paper_title: DemoFoundry: Toward Scalable Photorealistic Robot Data with Coding Agents and Generative Rendering

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Simulation-based synthesis faces a substantial visual gap relative to real environments, while video-only generation struggles to maintain physically consistent interactions and provide aligned action labels. We present DemoFoundry, an automated framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to synthesize photorealistic and physically grounded robot demonstrations. Coding agents both construct aligned real--proxy video pairs from existing robot episodes to train a video renderer and write executable interaction programs to generate new demonstrations. Given a scene reference and task instruction, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and writes a control program without requiring target-task human demonstrations. Program execution in a physics simulator produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The video renderer translates these proxy videos into scene-consistent, photorealistic observations, reducing the need for detailed appearance modeling in each scene. Automated task-execution checks select successful trajectories for rendering and policy learning. Experiments show improved visual quality and action--video consistency. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations.

sections.content: Scaling robot learning requires demonstrations that combine realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision. Policies trained on the generated demonstrations outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations. 1. Introduction Generalizable robot policies require large-scale training data covering diverse interactions between robots and their environments. Such data should pair realistic visual observations with reliable action supervision across broad range 1 of objects, scenes, and tasks. Human teleoperation provides these demonstrations but requires sustained operator effort to execute tasks and reset the environment between trials. Expanding interaction coverage therefore calls for scalable alternatives to manual collection. Simulation provides scalable source of robot interactions [7, 22, 50, 53]. However, simulated observations still exhibit substantial visual gap relative to real environments in object appearance, materials, lighting, and background detail. Domain randomization improves robustness to these differences [7, 46], although matching particular deployment environment remains challenging. Generative video models can synthesize realistic observations across diverse scenes, but their outputs often exhibit inconsistent contact, object motion, and task execution [11]. Video-only generation also lacks an executable control trace that directly supplies robot actions. Recovering action supervision through inverse dynamics introduces an additional estimation problem [25]. These complementary strengths motivate separating interaction generation from appearance synthesis [9]. Executable programs provide controllable source of behavior, and video rendering supplies scene appearance. Scaling this approach requires efficient construction of rendering supervision and task programs across scenes. Advances in program-based control and embodied reasoning [28, 42] make coding agents practical means of coordinating the reconstruction, alignment, and control tools involved in this process. We introduce DemoFoundry, an automated data engine combining coding agents and generative rendering, as illustrated in Fig. 1. First, pair-construction agent reconstructs and aligns existing real robot episodes with proxy videos, forming paired dataset for training video renderer. The renderer learns to recover appearance from scene reference while following robot and object motion. Second, for novel scene, an agent reconstructs task-relevant geometry and develops program to execute the instructed task. Executing this program under different object layouts in simulation produces proxy videos with aligned robot states and actions. The renderer then converts these proxy videos into photorealistic observations using the corresponding scene references. DemoFoundry enables zero-shot data generation for novel robot embodiments and scenes from reference images and robot/camera configurations, without target-scene demonstrations or human operator involvement during generation. We evaluate it on real-world platform across three manipulation tasks using Diffusion Policy and π0.5 [3, 10]. Our renderers improve visual quality over baselines while maintaining strong actionvideo consistency. Policies trained on our generated data outperform raw-simulation training and approach the performance of training on an equal number of real demonstrations. Policy performance improves with Table 1. Table 1 places these components within existing robot data-generation pipelines. We make three contributions. An automated data engine that couples coding-agent programs with appearance rendering to synthesize photorealistic, action-labeled robot demonstrations across diverse scenes and tasks without manual intervention during production. An agent-constructed dataset of 1,884 aligned realproxy video pairs from four public robot datasets, used to adapt two video-generation models for rendering newly programmed interactions. We plan to release the paired dataset upon publication. Real-robot experiments demonstrating improved policy learning over raw simulation and performance comparable to real-demonstration training, complemented by visualquality comparisons, paired-training ablation, and datascaling experiments. 2. Related Work 2.1. Programmatic Simulation and Data Engines Programmatic simulation scales robot demonstrations through automatic task specification and behavior generation. Language-model-based systems synthesize executable policies, task programs, and learning objectives [22, 28, 50, 53]. RoboTwin 2.0 combines feedback-driven expert-code generation with domain randomization for bimanual manipulation [7], while Genie Sim 3.0 provides high-fidelity simulation infrastructure and diverse assets [59]. DemoFoundry extends this paradigm by coupling agent-generated behavior with video renderer trained on aligned realproxy observations. Figure 2. DemoFoundry pipeline. (a) pair-construction agent writes and refines reconstruction, alignment, and simulation programs to convert diverse existing demonstrations into realproxy video pairs. (b) The paired dataset supervises video renderer conditioned on proxy video and an initial RGB reference frame. (c) In new scene, an agent builds task program and executes it under randomized simulator layouts. For successful executions, initial proxy frames guide matching RGB-reference generation before video rendering. Simulation retains actions and robot states for robot learning without new target-task demonstrations. 2.2. Robot Data Synthesis from Real Observations Real observations support data generation through trajectory reuse and scene reconstruction. Demonstration-amplification methods transform recorded motion into new object configurations [26, 32, 56], while replay and reconstructed-asset rendering expand visual and embodiment coverage [17, 60]. Digital-twin methods recover scene appearance and geometry for policy learning [19, 38, 48], and IGen generates visuomotor trajectories from open-world images [18]. Agentic Real2Sim automates episode reconstruction and physical replay, producing realsimulation correspondences [5]. DemoFoundry uses such correspondences across multiple robot datasets to train reusable video renderer, then generates new-task trajectories from scene references and task programs. 2.3. Generative Rendering for Robot Learning Generative models provide photorealistic observations for robot learning. DreamGen and EVA synthesize behavior videos and recover action supervision through inverse dynamics [25, 51]. Trajectory-conditioned approaches instead guide appearance synthesis with robot motion, edited geometry, or simulator controls [6, 57, 58, 63]. RoboTransfer uses multi-view geometric conditions [30], and RoboRender trains on real-derived depth and robot-mask controls paired with RGB videos [23]. Code World Model and SolarRenderer provide related program-driven and structuralvideo rendering mechanisms [9, 15]. Hybrid robot data engines combine executable programs with video rendering. ComSim [37] constructs realsimulation pairs by replaying recorded actions, while PyRUA-DataFarm [61] builds its target scene from one calibration episode. DemoFoundry connects agent-built, multi-source realproxy pairs to renderer adaptation and new-scene demonstration generation. 3. DemoFoundry 3.1. Overview and Formulation As illustrated in Fig. 2, DemoFoundry first constructs aligned realproxy video pairs to train video renderer, as detailed in Sec. 3.2. To generate demonstrations in new scene, coding agent takes reference image ref , robot specification defining the robot and gripper models, camera calibration specifying intrinsics and extrinsics, and task instruction ℓ to build simulated scene and task program p.

Given new scene reference ref , robot specification R, camera calibration C, and task instruction ℓ, GPT-6 Astra agent reconstructs taskrelevant assets using the procedure in Sec. 3.2. It imports the robot/gripper models and assembles the simulated scene E. Following code-based robot control [28] and simulation data engines [7, 50], the agent writes an executable task program using tool library for scene queries, grasp proposals, inverse kinematics, motion planning, and robot control. Video Renderer Training Agent-driven reconstruction. We construct realproxy video pairs from DROID [27], AgiBot World [43], RoboMIND [55], and RH20T [16] to supervise video renderer training. For each source episode, GPT-6 Astra agent [35] reconstructs the task-relevant scene from RGB observations, available depth, camera calibration, and robot/gripper records. It obtains object masks with SAM 3.1 [4] and fits the tabletop as the support surface. Simple objects are represented by parameterized shapes and converted into meshes through agent-written Blender Python scripts [21, 31]. Complex assets are reconstructed from RGB images and masks using SAM 3D Objects [8]. Available depth initializes scale and placement, which the agent refines using multi-view silhouettes, object orientation, and support constraints. The resulting visual and collision geometry preserves task-relevant openings and contact surfaces for physical replay. Physical execution and refinement. The reconstructed assets and corresponding robot/gripper models are assembled in physics engine, such as MuJoCo [47] or DexSim [14]. The agent replays the recorded actions through the robot controller, with contact dynamics determining object motion. Rendering the simulated trajectories at the recorded camera poses and timestamps yields candidate proxy videos. To align each proxy with its real-video counterpart, we compare object masks at sampled keyframes and require silhouette IoU of at least 0.80 for every visible object in every view. Algorithm 1 repeats this process until the target number of demonstrations has been collected in Dgen. Robot policy learning. We use Dgen to train Diffusion Policy [10] and π0.5 [3]. Both receive rendered observations and robot states as inputs, with aligned simulator actions as supervision and task instruction ℓ additionally supplied to π0.5. At deployment, the policies receive real camera observations and robot states. Section 4.1 and Appendix provide training and deployment settings. 5 4. Experiments 4.1. Implementation Details Video renderer training. We train two video renderers Gθ based on LTX-2.5 Layout-to-Render [29] and MiniMaxH3 Ref2VA [33], denoted Ours (LTX) and Ours (H3), respectively. Both are fine-tuned on our aligned realproxy pairs with source-balanced sampling while keeping the backbones and visual encoders frozen. LTX continues training the released rank-128 LoRA on 121-frame clips. H3 uses rank-32 attention LoRA on 158-frame clips at 24 fps, with frozen DeCFG correction [12] enabled during training and removed at inference. Training resolutions are 512 384 for AgiBot/RoboMIND and 640 352 for DROID/RH20T, expressed as widthheight. Appendix lists the training configurations. Inference settings. The autoregressive rollout in Sec. 3.3 uses 121-frame windows for LTX and 158-frame windows for H3. LTX uses 30 denoising steps with guidance scale 3, while H3 uses 50 steps with its native sampler. We use Qwen-Image-2.1 [39] for reference-image editing, with GPT Image 2.5 [36] as an alternative. The H3 rendering prompt, detailed in Appendix B, describes scene appearance and instructs the model to follow proxy motion. Appearance edits modify this prompt, whereas task instruction ℓ guides the agent and policy. Policy training. We use our synthetic demonstrations to train two downstream robot policies, Diffusion Policy (DP) [10] and π0.5 [3]. We fine-tune π0.5 from the pretrained π0.5-base weights for 20,000 steps with batch size of 32, and train DP for 50,000 steps with batch size of 64. On the real robot, π0.5 receives three camera views and joint/gripper states; both policies run at 25 Hz. Appendix gives the action representation and optimization settings. 4.2. Visual Fidelity Baselines. Raw simulation directly uses the proxy video. General conditional baselines include Wan2.2-Fun-5BControl [1] with structural-video controls, LTX-2.5 Layoutto-Render [29] with layout/reference conditioning, and MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [33] with image/video references. Cosmos-Transfer2.5 [34] provides spatially controlled simto-real appearance transfer. RoboTransfer [30] uses depth, normals, and appearance references, and RoboRender [23] uses depth, robot RGB masks, text, and previous-frame conditioning. Required geometry controls come from the same simulated trajectories. Released and adapted LTX/H3 variants use matched inputs and sampling settings. Quantitative results. As shown in Table 3, our H3 renderer performs best across all four metrics, improving EventAlign from 80.95% to 95.23% over the released H3 model. 4.3. Real-Robot Policy Learning We evaluate robot policy learning on TianJi Marvin M6S (CCS-696) dual-arm platform [45], new embodiment for our demonstration-generation pipeline shown in Fig. 5. Unless otherwise specified, subsequent experiments use our fine-tuned H3 renderer for data generation. We evaluate three real-world manipulation tasks: placing can into tray, stacking blocks, and inserting pen into pen holder. We train Diffusion Policy [10] as visuomotor baseline and π0.5 [3] as the VLA policy separately for each task. Success requires the specified placement or stack to remain stable after release. Table 4 compares five data conditions with 30 realrobot trials per task and policy. Simulation-only and DemoFoundry-only share 50 trajectories per task, differing only in visual observations; real-only uses 50 human demonstrations. Mixed conditions add 100 raw or H3-rendered trajectories to the same real data. We report success counts and mean success across tasks. DemoFoundry-only training improves mean success over raw simulation by 34.4 percentage points for DP and 32.2 for π0.5. Adding 100 raw-simulation trajectories has little effect on mean success relative to real-only training, changing it by 1.1 percentage points for DP and +1.1 for π0.5. Adding generated demonstrations to real data further improves over real-only training by 23.3 and 20.0 percentage points, respectively. 4.4. Generalization across Scene Variations Using video model as the renderer enables domain randomization through changes to the rendering prompt. We evaluate the resulting policy generalization with π0.5 on the can-to-tray task under three appearance variations covered during training: green bottle, changed background color, and altered lighting. We compare policies trained on simulation domain randomization [7, 46] and DemoFoundry data with language-prompted visual variations. Object placements are randomized on every trial. Over 30 real-robot trials per condition, DemoFoundry achieves 21, 22, and 18 successes, compared with 5, 10, and 2 for Simulation + DR. These results demonstrate stronger visual generalization than standard simulation domain randomization. Appendix reports the settings and results. 5. Conclusion We present DemoFoundry, framework that couples coding agents with generative rendering to automate the synthesis of photorealistic, action-labeled robot demonstrations. Experiments demonstrate improved visual quality, strong actionvideo consistency, and effective policy learning on real robots. Remaining challenges include multi-view consistency and drift over repeated autoregressive rollouts, which may be mitigated by joint multi-view generation and memory-based conditioning across video segments. DemoFoundry offers path to generating diverse robot interactions on demand with reduced human collection effort, enabling scalable training of more generalizable robot policies.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: OpenAI Codex assisted with literature search and language polishing. Within DemoFoundry, GPT-6 Astra supports scene reconstruction and task programming, Qwen-Image2.1 generates reference images, and LTX-2.5 and MiniMaxH3 render demonstration videos, as detailed in Sections 34 and the appendix. The authors take full responsibility for the submission.

sections.title: Supplementary Material
sections.content: A. Coding Agent Harness The harness connects GPT-6 Astra to reconstruction, simulation, and evaluation tools. Realproxy mask comparisons guide scene reconstruction; execution errors and taskcompletion checks guide task programming. Successful programs are reused across randomized layouts. Table S1 summarizes these feedback loops. Table S1. Execution feedback in the coding agent harness. Feedback guides scene reconstruction in main Sec. 3.2 and task programming in main Sec. 3.3. Source-episode reconstruction New-task programming Execution Replay the recorded controls in the reconstructed scene with the original camera calibration. Feedback and revision silhouette mismatch identifies an object, camera view, and keyframe. Revise the objects geometry, scale, or initial pose and replay the same controls. Acceptance and output Keep the realproxy pair if every visible objects silhouette IoU is at least 0.80 in every checked view and keyframe. Discard it if it still fails after three refinement rounds. Run the agent-written program in scene using the robot-control tools in . Execution errors or failed task-completion check guide revisions to p. Test the revised program in the simulator. Reuse successful program across randomized layouts. For each successful rollout, send Pi to rendering and retain the aligned states Qi and actions Ai. Tool library . Reconstruction interfaces. Observation and calibration readers establish coordinate and time mappings. Assetbuilding tools fit task geometry and contact surfaces; robot/gripper checks verify transforms and gripper-opening calibration. Native replay returns simulated trajectories, while image-space comparisons localize alignment errors. Tool library (continued). Task-programming interfaces. Scene queries return current object poses. Grasp proposals, inverse kinematics, motion planning, and robot-control interfaces support program p. Execution returns task-completion feedback and synchronized proxy videos , states Q, and actions A. Effect of reconstruction feedback. Table S2 evaluates the initial replay and up to three refinement rounds on fixed, source-balanced set of episodes. An episode passes when every visible object achieves silhouette IoU 0.80 across all checked views and keyframes. Pass rates are computed cumulatively over all attempted episodes with fixed calibration, segmentation, and controls, while alignment metrics are evaluated on held-out keyframes. Across three rounds, iterative refinement raises the acceptance rate from 33.1% to 39.7%, improves mean mask IoU from 0.517 to 0.601, reduces track error from 1.370% to 0.956%, and increases motion correlation to 0.932. Table S2. Episode acceptance and alignment by refinement round. Mask IoU measures silhouette overlap. Track error is the mean real/proxy centroid distance as percentage of the image diagonal. Motion correlation is the Pearson correlation of horizontal and vertical centroid displacements over jointly visible intervals. Reconstruction stage Initial replay +1 refinement +2 refinements +3 refinements Pass rate Mask Track error Motion corr. IoU (%) (%) 33.1 35.3 36.8 39.7 0.517 0.554 0.568 0.601 1.370 1.214 1.082 0.956 0.893 0.907 0.919 0. B. Renderer and Policy Implementation Table S3 lists the renderer settings, and Table S4 gives the H3 rendering prompt. Adjacent inference windows overlap by one frame, giving strides of 120 frames for LTX and 157 for H3. 13 Table S3. Video renderer training and inference settings. Paired samples are split into 96% training, 2% validation, and 2% test data. Sizes are widthheight. Six-part H3 rendering prompt. The native configuration identifies the RGB reference as <Image 1> and the proxy as <Video 1>. The task instruction ℓ is used for programming and policy learning. Appearance edits modify the descriptive and retention clauses. Section Prompt text subject definitions summary retention analysis detailed description overall soundscape non diegetic music <Video 1> is simplified simulation rendering of the robot and task geometry, from the same camera as the target video. <Image 1> is the appearance reference image for the first frame of [Shot 1]. [keyframe completion + reference generation] The target video begins from <Image 1> and follows the frame-by-frame structure and motion of <Video 1>. photographic recording of robot manipulation scene, matching the supplied first frame and following the supplied structure sequence. <Video 1> (frame-by-frame layout, shapes, character poses and motion, camera): attribute transfer - the layout, shapes, poses, motion and camera are followed exactly; materials, colours and lighting are not given by <Video 1> and are the target videos own; the simplified simulation materials and plain background of <Video 1> is not shown. <Image 1> ([Shot 1] first frame): fully preserved - the composition, subjects, materials, colours and lighting of <Image 1> are the target videos first frame. [Shot 1] The shot begins from <Image 1>. The target is continuous photographic recording of the robot workspace shown in the first frame. Preserve the robots visible identity, link shapes, gripper, table surface, task objects, room background, materials, colours and lighting. Follow only the poses, motion, occlusion and object trajectories visible in the structure sequence in playback order. Keep the camera viewpoint and any camera motion consistent with that sequence. Maintain the actual photographic background throughout the clip. Preserve object count and connected robot geometry. Do not introduce new action or an unseen object. Keep textures and illumination stable as the robot moves. N/A N/A 14 Table S5. Policy training and deployment settings. Settings are fixed across data conditions. The π0.5 interface maps three camera views and 16 joint/gripper coordinates to its 32-dimensional representation. States and actions use training-set quantile normalization. Arm targets are joint offsets, and gripper targets are absolute values. C. Domain Randomization and Generalization Figure S1. Simulation randomization and prompt-controlled rendering. The leftmost column shows the original appearance. Subsequent columns compare green bottle, wood-grain tabletop, blue background, and cyan/magenta lighting. The top row shows domain randomization in simulation; the bottom row shows appearance variations generated by changing the rendering prompt in DemoFoundry. Training data. Figure S1 illustrates two ways to vary the appearance of demonstration. For Simulation + DR, we manually configure object and tabletop materials, background colors, and lighting in the simulator. With DemoFoundry, editing the appearance prompt lets the video renderer produce photorealistic variations from the same RGB reference and proxy video. Real-robot evaluation. We evaluate π0.5 on the can-totray task under three target visual variations covered by the respective randomization pipelines: green bottle, changed background color, and altered lighting. Object placements are randomized on every trial, with 30 real-robot trials per policy per condition. Table S6. Generalization on the can-to-tray task. Entries report π0.5 successes out of 30 real-robot trials per condition. Training data Green bottle Simulation + DR DemoFoundry 5/30 21/30 Background color 10/30 22/30 Lighting 2/30 18/30 As reported in Table S6, DemoFoundry outperforms Simulation + DR across all three settings, achieving 18/30 versus 2/30 successes under altered lighting. 15 D. RealProxy Video Pairs Figure S2. Realproxy pairs from DROID and RH20T. The first six rows show DROID episodes and the last four show RH20T episodes. Each row presents three time-aligned realproxy pairs in chronological order. Figure S3. Realproxy pairs from AgiBot and RoboMIND. The first three rows show AgiBot episodes and the last three show RoboMIND episodes. Each row presents three time-aligned realproxy pairs in chronological order, with head/front and wrist views grouped in each cell. 17 E. Temporal Generation Comparisons Figures S4S7 present qualitative temporal comparisons on held-out episodes across the four source datasets, where H3 and LTX denote the released MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA and LTX-2.5 Layout-to-Render models, respectively. Figure S4. MiniMax-H3 rendering of bottle transfer and fruit placement. Released H3 retains proxy-like colors and introduces gripper absent from the real fruit-placement frames. Paired adaptation improves scene appearance and gripperobject correspondence. Figure S5. MiniMax-H3 rendering of tape-roll pickup and block manipulation. Released H3 retains simplified simulation backgrounds, whereas paired adaptation recovers the wooden tabletop and blue work mat. 19 Figure S6. LTX rendering of fruit washing and hair-dryer manipulation. Released LTX distorts object shapes in the wrist views, whereas paired adaptation better preserves fruit appearance and hair-dryer shape. 20 Figure S7. LTX rendering of fruit handling and bread transfer. Released LTX introduces texture artifacts and blurs the bread and gripper in wrist views, whereas paired adaptation produces clearer object boundaries and more consistent scene appearance.
